title: Longest increasing subsequence: subset enumeration vs quadratic DP vs patience sorting
problem_statement: Given a list a[0..n-1] of n integers, compute the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence: the largest k for which there are indices i_1 < ... < i_k with a[i_1] < ... < a[i_k] (0 for the empty list).

input.size_measure: n integers of bounded size; each comparison is O(1).

algorithms.name: subset enumeration
algorithms.idea: Enumerate all 2^n subsets of indices as bitmasks, test each for being strictly increasing with one scan over the n positions, and keep the largest size.
algorithms.pseudocode: best = 0; for mask in 0..2^n-1: scan i = 0..n-1, for the i in mask check a[i] > previous chosen value; if increasing: best = max(best, popcount(mask)); return best
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(2^n n) on every input (each of the 2^n masks is scanned over all n positions, with no early exit)
algorithms.correctness: Exhaustive: every subsequence corresponds to exactly one index subset.

algorithms.name: quadratic dynamic programming
algorithms.idea: L[i] = length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence ending at position i = 1 + max L[j] over j < i with a[j] < a[i]; the answer is max L.
algorithms.pseudocode: for i in 0..n-1: L[i] = 1 + max({L[j] : j < i, a[j] < a[i]} or {0}); return max(L or {0})
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) on every input: n(n-1)/2 comparisons
algorithms.correctness: An increasing subsequence ending at i is either a[i] alone or an increasing subsequence ending at some j < i with a[j] < a[i], extended by a[i]; optimal substructure gives the recurrence (CLRS Exercise 15.4-5).

algorithms.name: patience sorting with binary search
algorithms.idea: Maintain tails[k] = the smallest possible last element of a strictly increasing subsequence of length k + 1 seen so far. tails is strictly increasing, so each new element replaces the first entry >= it (found by binary search) or is appended; the answer is len(tails).
algorithms.pseudocode: tails = []; for x in a: k = first index with tails[k] >= x (binary search); if k = len(tails): append x else tails[k] = x; return len(tails)
algorithms.time_complexity: O(n log L) <= O(n log n), L = the answer; Theta(n log n) in the worst case, e.g. on increasing input (L = n), which is the V2 scaling input
algorithms.correctness: Invariant: after reading a prefix, tails[k] is the minimum last element over all strictly increasing subsequences of length k + 1 in that prefix, and tails is strictly increasing; placing x at the first entry >= x preserves this. This is the first row of Schensted's insertion (Schensted 1961); its length is the LIS length.

relationship: Enumerating all 2^n subsequences is exponential. The DP over 'best subsequence ending at i' needs only Theta(n^2) (the T2 step). Keeping only the minimal tail for each length, which is a sorted array, replaces the linear inner scan with a binary search: O(n log n) (the T3 step).

verification.method: V1: all three implementations agree with each other and with an independent oracle (in harness.py): the LIS length equals the LCS length of a and sorted(set(a)), computed by the textbook LCS table, for n <= 400. Inputs are random lists with many ties (so strictness matters) plus sorted, reversed and constant lists, n = 0..14 (subset enumeration up to n = 14), 30, 100, 400 and 1500 (quadratic DP up to n = 1500; at n = 1500 only the DP and patience sorting are compared). V2 uses strictly increasing lists with random gaps, the worst case for patience sorting; the other two do the same work on every input of length n. Runtimes fit 2^n n (n = 10..16), n^2 (n = 100..1600) and n log n (n = 1000..100000). At the default tolerance 0.25 a fit against n alone would also pass for patience sorting, so V2 confirms near-linear growth rather than isolating the log factor.

caveats: Patience sorting costs Theta(n log L) for answer L. On increasing input (used for V2) that is Theta(n log n). On uniformly random permutations L / sqrt(n) -> 2 (Logan & Shepp 1977; Vershik & Kerov 1977), and log L ~ (1/2) log n is still Theta(log n). Fredman (1975) analyses the comparison complexity of computing the LIS length; we record no lower bound from it because the paper's exact statement has not been checked here. The subset enumeration deliberately has no early exit, so its Theta(2^n n) holds on every input.
notes: The quadratic DP is the standard textbook dynamic program; the O(n log n) method is often called patience sorting, after the card game. LIS is also LCS(a, sorted(set(a))), the reduction used by the V1 oracle; see lcs-brute-vs-dp.
